adverse impact. However, that site is not  
 
[2:16:36 PM] 
 
held accountable for the drainage impacts created by the existing impervious cover. So to correct this, 
the ldc revision carries forward the previously proposed green field standard, which requires that 
redeveloping sites manage their storm water as if they had no impervious cover. There is also a new 
provision for small sites which we will discuss next. The green field standard ensures that 
redevelopment and development on a green field site are treated equally. Both must provide or 
contribute to drainage problems or drainage solutions to address drainage problems in a manner that is 
proportionate to their impacts on the drainage system. This change will reduce flood risk citywide, 
including in areas with existing problems. Providing these detention or conveyance upgrades will also

few pictures that illustrate what we're talking about.  
 
[2:17:36 PM]

fund other regional solutions under what's called the regional storm water management program. We 
recognize that the green field standard is a significant new requirement for redevelopment sites and we 
can cognizant of council's direction for non-zoning regulations to allow for higher yields in centers and

Council direction also calls for fiscally sound infrastructure investment  
 
[2:18:36 PM] 
 
that maximizes public investment and minimizes long-term obligations. We've also heard that the green

[2:19:36 PM]

[2:20:37 PM] 
 
improvements. Those off site improvements are more likely to provide a significant drainage benefit

watersheds. The current proposal also revises the variance findings to allow staff to recommend

and/or remove exceptions to impervious cover limits in the redevelopment exceptions and to provide

The existing water quality code includes three redevelopment exceptions. One for urban and suburban

these redevelopment exceptions is to allow environmentally non-compliant properties to redevelop 
their existing impervious cover in exchange for providing water quality treatment and in some 
watersheds, off site open space preservation. Most of the older properties that were developed before 
the city adopted water quality protections, do not comply with the watershed impervious cover limits,

To come into compliance with

current code standards, many of these properties would need to remove a very large amount of existing 
development. It has been suggested that the central provision of the redevelopment exceptions, which

the ldc protection, drainage improvements that will be required of redeveloping sites. Models are also

Williamson creek. All of the old untreated sites like this one are sending pollution straight into a creek

used. Only three projects have used it in the 12 years since it was adopted in 2007. Since the outcome of 
each redevelopment project is improved water quality on existing gray fields sites rather than clearing 
trees and vegetation from natural green field sites, plus the wide array of other benefits that I

development to use the Barton springs zone redevelopment exception. So first up is a proposal to

Next is a proposal to  
 
[2:35:48 PM] 
 
streamline the approval process. In the Barton springs zone and water supply watersheds, this proposal

exception. The current triggers include having more than 25 dwelling units, being located outside of the

redevelopment site rather than its water quality impacts. The redevelopment exceptions do not waive

[2:36:49 PM]

and hopefully encourage more properties to use the redevelopment exception. And finally, the ldc
